attempt.boards_note: Each board is the learner's committed probability distribution AFTER that stage's evidence reveal (design/07 steps 2/4). Boards must sum to 1; the checker enforces it.

debrief_text.analysis: Three teaching points, each tied to a scored component. (1) The operative history is evidence — the loudest in the case. 'The injury was recognised and drained' was the learner's reason for discounting it; but drain-and-refer (trace-02, dp4) is a temporising pathway, not a repair: the transected duct was still transected on day 4. The consider-the-opposite prompt (design/07): 'if this is the injury I already know about, what would the stone story have to explain away?' — the clips, the cut-off, and the recognised class III mechanism, at minimum. (2) Sequence the anatomy before the therapy: C14 makes MRCP the gold standard for morphological evaluation and classification of a bile duct injury, and states ERCP's limits in exactly this anatomy — it cannot opacity ducts upstream of a complete obstruction and cannot bridge a transection. Ordered at stage 2 as treatment for an unproven stone, the ERCP is scored non-contributory: it changed no board, no criterion, and no classification input that the record did not already establish, at an invasive procedure's risk. (3) Criteria discipline held where it mattered: TG18 cholangitis reads B and C satisfied but A unmet (afebrile, WBC 8.9, CRP 8) at every stage — not suspected, mechanically — while remaining the case's live risk, which is why the disposition arms surveillance and names the drainage route (PTBD, for complete obstruction) that fever would trigger.
debrief_text.description: Stage by stage: the workbench leads with the bile duct injury from stage 1 (0.35, its declared prior — the operative history is stage-1 evidence, not backstory) and never gives up the lead. The learner leads with the stone (0.40), raises it on the cholestatic panel (0.45) as if cholestasis discriminated between obstruction causes — it does not; it is shared by all of them — and orders ERCP at stage 2 as therapy, before any cross-sectional anatomy exists. The ERCP returns a cut-off at surgical clips, a clear distal duct, and nothing to treat; the learner still holds the stone at 0.30 ('above the clips, where ERCP cannot see'). Only the stage-4 MRCP closes it: no stone in any duct, and the workbench's one quantified update (LR- 0.0794, C15) carries the stone to 0.0195, across the rule-out line. The learner commits to the injury (0.60) — but still parks 0.25 on the stone, which is the attempt's anchoring event. Learner Brier: 0.7550 -> 0.7118 -> 0.4148 -> 0.2306. The workbench Brier is flat at 0.5150 until the MRCP (0.4053): this case carries exactly one likelihood ratio, and the rest of its reasoning honestly runs through the criteria and classification blocks rather than through invented numbers.
debrief_text.reactions: The attempt reaches the right diagnosis, the right classification, and the right disposition — and its opening panel (inflammatory markers, cholestasis panel, ultrasound) is exactly the panel C14 prescribes. Between those bookends it commits the error this case was built to expose: it falls for the treatable diagnosis. A retained stone is the cause of postoperative jaundice that ERCP can fix, so the stone is what the learner goes looking for — past an operative history that already contains the answer.
debrief_text.summary: Diagnosis: major bile duct injury — complete transection of the common bile duct at the index operation (Theatre trace-02), classified by the case's own block from the staged findings as Strasberg E1 / Bismuth I (stump 25 mm below an intact confluence). Disposition as committed: hepatobiliary-centre care, no endoscopic therapy for a transection, Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy after a minimum of 3 weeks (C14 statement 7.4 — the 72 h to 3 week band), cholangitis surveillance meanwhile. Calibration note: a calibration curve is a property of a case SERIES (design/07); the series now has two cases and eight staged learner Brier scores (case 1: 0.4550 -> 0.0276; this case: 0.7550 -> 0.2306 — the gap between those endpoints is, in large part, the price of the anchor), and claims nothing more.

attempt.learner: Model learner — an authored attempt shipped with the case as its worked example, in the same role as Milestone 17's shipped traces and case 1's model learner. It is deliberately imperfect in one documented way: it anchors on a retained common bile duct stone — the treatable diagnosis — ordering ERCP at stage 2 as therapy before the anatomy is defined, and it keeps the stone at 0.25 at stage 4, after the MRCP it finally ordered has shown no stone anywhere and the workbench has ruled the stone out. Its stage-2 reasoning ('the injury was recognised and drained; jaundice this deep is a stone until proven otherwise') inverts the case's own operative history. Everything else it does is sound: the right first panel, the right ultrasound, and — once the MRCP is in front of it — the right commitment and the right WSES-timed disposition.

stages.board_rationale: The learner leads with the retained stone (0.40): 'post-cholecystectomy jaundice is a retained stone until proven otherwise — and ERCP fixes it.' The bile duct injury is on the board (0.25) because the referral letter states it, but it is discounted: 'the injury was recognised and drained at the time.'
stages.orders_note: The right first panel: inflammatory markers, the cholestasis panel, and the collection/dilatation ultrasound (C14 statements 6.2-6.3).

stages.board_rationale: The cholestatic panel and dilated ducts RAISE the stone to 0.45 — read as confirmation. The injury rises only to 0.30. Cholangitis is correctly not chased (afebrile, sub-threshold markers), and hepatocellular injury correctly fades on the pattern.
stages.orders_note: The attempt's pivotal error: ERCP ordered as therapy for the presumed stone before any cross-sectional anatomy exists. MRCP — available from this stage, non-invasive, and the classification's source — is not ordered.

stages.board_rationale: The ERCP shows a cut-off at surgical clips with a clear distal duct and nothing extracted — yet the stone is still held at 0.30 ('a stone could sit in the proximal stump, above the clips, where ERCP cannot see'). The injury takes the lead (0.45) but the anchor is visible: the learner is defending the stone against the evidence rather than updating on it.
stages.orders_note: The right order, one stage late: the gold-standard morphological study (C14) that should have preceded the invasive one.

stages.board_rationale: MRCP: complete transection, stump 25 mm, no stone in any duct. The learner commits to the bile duct injury (0.60) and the correct disposition — but still parks 0.25 on the retained stone, one stage after the only quantified test in the case has ruled it out on the workbench (posterior 0.0195). This is the attempt's anchoring event, recorded by rule in the debrief.

commit.management: HPB-centre pathway as the case's management block specifies: no endoscopic therapy for a complete transection; definitive Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy after a minimum of 3 weeks (C14 statement 7.4), with cholangitis surveillance and the drain monitored meanwhile.
